title: No other gods
hookLine: first loyalty to the one God, before money, work or fame

lines: THE FIRST HOUR, THE FIRST DOLLAR.
cards: A bank statement, a calendar and a screen-time report. Lay them side by side and they tell a story: what got the first hour of the day, the first dollar of the paycheck, the first worry of the morning.
The first commandment asks about the same thing in older words. "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." There may be no statue in the house.
But money, work, fame and other people's approval all know how to ask for first place, and they ask politely.

teach.b: The commandment doesn't open with a rule. It opens with a rescue. "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage."
First God says what God has done; then comes the word. Loyalty is an answer to a rescue.
Some readers point out that before me can also be heard as before my face, in my presence: nothing else gets to stand in the room as if it were God.
Jesus names one rival plainly, as day 252 heard: "No man can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon." Mammon is wealth, money treated like a master. He doesn't say money is evil.
He says it can't share the throne. You end up serving one and using the other.

teach.h: WHAT DOES YOUR HEART CLING TO?
teach.b: Martin Luther, explaining this commandment in his Large Catechism, turned it into a question: whatever your heart clings to and relies on, that is really your god. That makes the commandment a mirror.
A rival god might be a career, a reputation, a child's success, a bank balance, your own competence. Good things, often. The trouble isn't that they matter.
It's when they get the first hour, the deepest trust and the final word.

teach.h: THE SPRING THE OTHERS FLOW FROM.
teach.b: Luther also said this first commandment is the spring the others flow from. Put God first, the reading goes, and the other loyalties fall into their places, loved better, not less.

how: Christians learn this commandment in catechism, often with Luther's explanation in Lutheran churches, and some examine themselves against it before confession or communion by asking what they have put in God's place.

o: a rule that only one church may worship God
a ban on learning about other religions' beliefs
letting nothing but God hold first place in your life

games.q: the first word — tap the pairs.
p: also heard as before my face
I am the LORD thy God
what does your heart cling to?

s: the first commandment opens with a rule
it opens with a rescue: "which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt."
he says "ye cannot serve God and mammon": it can't share the throne.
for Luther, your god is whatever your heart clings to
his explanation turns the first commandment into a mirror.

games.q: you try to serve two masters at once, giving each exactly half. what does Jesus say happens?
o: you end up loving one and despising the other.
games.why: "either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon."

practice: Ask Luther's question slowly: what does my heart cling to, what do I check first in the morning, chew on last at night, trust to keep me safe?
Let one honest answer surface, even a good thing, and name it plainly, noticing how much it's been asked to carry. If you pray, you can hand it back to God in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: No other gods. The first word: loyalty to the one God who rescued, with nothing else allowed to take that first place.

orig.note: Hebrew: other gods. The words of Exodus 20:3.

carryVoice: Your line: first things first. It was day 394's line too, and it still holds. See you tomorrow.
